families.name: Asteraceae
families.tip: What looks like one flower is a head of many tiny florets, often with strap-shaped rays round the edge and a ring of green bracts beneath. Dandelions, thistles, daisies, ragworts.

families.name: Rosaceae
families.tip: Usually 5 separate petals, many stamens and leafy stipules at the base of the leaf stalk; fruits often fleshy (hips, haws, brambles, cherries).

families.name: Poaceae
families.tip: Round, usually hollow stems with solid joints; long narrow leaves with a sheath wrapping the stem and a small flap (ligule) where blade meets sheath. Flowers in tiny green spikelets.

families.name: Fabaceae
families.tip: Pea-flowers: a large upper petal, two side wings and a boat-shaped keel. Leaves usually compound, often with tendrils; fruit a pod.

families.name: Cyperaceae
families.tip: Grass-like, but stems usually solid and triangular ('sedges have edges'); leaves in three ranks with no ligule flap. Cotton-grasses and spike-rushes belong here too.

families.name: Brassicaceae
families.tip: Four petals in a cross, six stamens (four long, two short); fruit a pod that splits from the bottom, leaving a papery central wall. Often a cress-like taste.

families.name: Caryophyllaceae
families.tip: Leaves in opposite pairs on stems swollen at the joints; five petals, often notched or deeply split (stitchworts, campions, chickweeds).

families.name: Apiaceae
families.tip: Tiny flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters (umbels), usually white; leaves often finely divided with a sheathing base; stems often hollow and ridged. Some are very poisonous.

families.name: Lamiaceae
families.tip: Square stems, opposite leaves, two-lipped flowers in rings up the stem; many smell when crushed (mints, dead-nettles, thymes).

families.name: Plantaginaceae
families.tip: A mixed family: plantains (ribbed leaves, brown flower spikes), speedwells (4 blue petals, 2 stamens), foxglove, toadflaxes, water-starworts.

families.name: Ranunculaceae
families.tip: Many stamens and separate petals or petal-like sepals; leaves often deeply lobed; fruit a cluster of small dry seeds. Buttercups, anemones, columbines, Clematis.

families.name: Orchidaceae
families.tip: Six petal-like parts, the lowest forming a distinctive lip, often patterned or spurred; leaves with parallel veins, sometimes spotted.

families.name: Polygonaceae
families.tip: A papery sheath (ochrea) round the stem above each leaf base; small flowers, 3 to 6 parts; fruit a 3-sided nut. Docks, sorrels, knotweeds, bistorts.

families.name: Amaranthaceae
families.tip: Small green flowers in dense clusters; leaves often mealy or fleshy; plants of bare and salty ground (goosefoots, oraches, glassworts).

families.name: Boraginaceae
families.tip: Rough, bristly hairs; flowers in coiled sprays that unroll as they open, often turning from pink to blue (forget-me-nots, comfreys, borage).

families.name: Amaryllidaceae
families.tip: Six-petalled flowers from a papery sheath; leaves strap-like from a bulb. Onions and garlics (umbels, onion smell), daffodils (with a trumpet), snowdrops.

families.name: Orobanchaceae
families.tip: Semi-parasites (eyebright, yellow-rattle, cow-wheat, lousewort) with two-lipped flowers; broomrapes have no green at all.

families.name: Ericaceae
families.tip: Small evergreen shrubs with bell- or urn-shaped flowers; leaves often tiny, needle-like or leathery (heathers, bilberry, rhododendron).

families.name: Juncaceae
families.tip: Grass-like; rushes have round stems, often filled with white pith; woodrushes have flat, hairy-edged leaves. Flowers small, brown, six-parted.

families.name: Iridaceae
families.tip: Sword-shaped leaves in a flat fan; showy flowers with 6 parts and 3 stamens (irises, crocuses, montbretia).

families.name: Asparagaceae
families.tip: Bulb or rhizome plants with parallel-veined leaves and six-parted flowers: bluebell, lily-of-the-valley, Solomon's-seal, butcher's-broom.

families.name: Geraniaceae
families.tip: Five separate petals and a long beak-like fruit (the 'crane's bill'); leaves usually lobed like a hand or finely divided.

families.name: Campanulaceae
families.tip: Bell-shaped, usually blue flowers; milky sap; ovary below the flower (harebell, bellflowers, sheep's-bit).

families.name: Primulaceae
families.tip: Five petals joined at the base, with the stamens opposite the petal lobes (primroses, cowslips, loosestrifes, scarlet pimpernel).

families.name: Crassulaceae
families.tip: Thick, fleshy, water-storing leaves; star-shaped flowers. Walls, rocks and dry places (stonecrops, houseleek, navelwort).

families.name: Caprifoliaceae
families.tip: Opposite leaves; includes honeysuckle, teasels and scabiouses (flower heads), valerians and snowberry.

families.name: Aspleniaceae
families.tip: Ferns: no flowers; fronds uncurl from a crozier and carry spore patches underneath. Spleenworts, lady-fern, hard-fern, bladder-ferns.

families.name: Papaveraceae
families.tip: Poppies: 4 crumpled petals, many stamens, often milky or coloured sap. Fumitories and corydalis have small tubular, spurred flowers.

families.name: Saxifragaceae
families.tip: Small plants of rocks, mountains and damp places; five petals, often white; leaves frequently in a basal rosette. Golden-saxifrages have no petals.

families.name: Potamogetonaceae
families.tip: Water plants with floating or submerged leaves and small green flower spikes held above the water.

families.name: Onagraceae
families.tip: Four petals and a long, thin ovary below the flower; seeds often with silky hairs (willowherbs, evening-primroses, enchanter's-nightshade has 2 petals).

families.name: Salicaceae
families.tip: Trees and shrubs with catkins, male and female on separate plants; seeds with cottony hairs.

families.name: Rubiaceae
families.tip: Leaves in whorls (rings) of 4 to 12 round square stems; tiny 4-petalled flowers. Cleavers is the sticky one.

families.name: Polypodiaceae
families.tip: Ferns: no flowers. Buckler-ferns, male-fern, shield-ferns and polypodies, with round spore patches on the frond underside.

families.name: Hypericaceae
families.tip: Opposite leaves, often with see-through dots when held up to the light; yellow flowers with many stamens in bundles.

families.name: Euphorbiaceae
families.tip: Spurges have milky sap and odd cup-like green flower clusters with no petals; dog's mercury has small green flowers on spikes.

families.name: Plumbaginaceae
families.tip: Coastal plants with leaves in a basal rosette; pink or lavender flowers with papery calyces (thrift heads, sea-lavender sprays).

families.name: Gentianaceae
families.tip: Hairless plants with opposite leaves and petals joined into a tube with 4 to 5 spreading lobes (centauries, gentians, yellow-wort).

families.name: Scrophulariaceae
families.tip: Figworts have square stems and small brown two-lipped flowers; mulleins have tall spikes of yellow flowers and often woolly leaves. Buddleja belongs here.

families.name: Araceae
families.tip: Lords-and-ladies: a hooded leaf-like spathe round a club-shaped spike, then red berries. Duckweeds (tiny floating green discs) are in this family too.

families.name: Oxalidaceae
families.tip: Clover-like leaves of three heart-shaped leaflets that fold down at night; five petals; sharp-tasting.

families.name: Solanaceae
families.tip: Five petals joined into a star or bell, with stamens forming a cone in the centre; fruit a berry or capsule. Many poisonous (bittersweet, deadly nightshade, henbane).

families.name: Violaceae
families.tip: Five unequal petals, the lowest with a backward spur; leaves often heart-shaped (violets and pansies).

families.name: Aizoaceae
families.tip: Introduced succulents with thick, three-sided or cylindrical leaves and large daisy-like flowers with many narrow petals; coastal cliffs.

families.name: Malvaceae
families.tip: Mallows: five notched petals and a central column of stamens; fruit like a round cheese. Limes are trees with a strap-like bract on the flower stalk.

families.name: Hydrocharitaceae
families.tip: Water plants: frogbit (floating, kidney-shaped leaves, 3 white petals), water-soldier, and the submerged waterweeds with whorled leaves.

families.name: Alismataceae
families.tip: Wetland plants with long-stalked basal leaves and flowers with 3 white or pale pink petals (water-plantains, arrowhead).

families.name: Araliaceae
families.tip: Ivy: evergreen climber with lobed leaves on climbing stems and ball-shaped umbels of greenish flowers in autumn. Marsh pennywort has round, umbrella-like leaves.

families.name: Lentibulariaceae
families.tip: Insect-catching plants: butterworts have sticky, pale green leaf rosettes; bladderworts float in water with tiny bladder traps.

families.name: Betulaceae
families.tip: Trees and shrubs with catkins in late winter or spring; fruits are nuts (hazel), tiny winged seeds (birch) or woody 'cones' (alder).

families.name: Pinaceae
families.tip: Conifers with needles (single, in pairs or in bunches) and woody cones (pines, spruces, firs, larch).

families.name: Liliaceae
families.tip: Bulb plants with large six-petalled flowers and parallel-veined leaves (fritillary, tulips, lilies, yellow star-of-Bethlehem).

families.name: Equisetaceae
families.tip: No flowers; jointed, ridged stems with rings of tiny teeth and whorls of thin green branches; spores in a cone at the stem tip.

families.name: Viburnaceae
families.tip: Shrubs with opposite leaves and flat-topped clusters of small white flowers, then berries (elder, guelder-rose, wayfaring-tree). Moschatel is a small herb.

families.name: Asphodelaceae
families.tip: Mostly introduced: New Zealand flax (huge leathery sword leaves), red-hot pokers, day-lilies; six-parted flowers.

families.name: Typhaceae
families.tip: Tall water-edge plants with long flat leaves: bulrushes have brown sausage-shaped heads; bur-reeds have spiky green balls.

families.name: Convolvulaceae
families.tip: Twining climbers with funnel-shaped flowers and arrow-shaped leaves. Dodders are leafless pink threads with no green.

families.name: Fagaceae
families.tip: Trees with catkins; fruit a nut in a cup or husk (acorns, beech-mast, sweet chestnuts).

families.name: Oleaceae
families.tip: Opposite leaves; flowers with 4 joined petals and 2 stamens, or no petals in ash. Ash has winged 'keys'; privet has black berries.

families.name: Sapindaceae
families.tip: Trees with opposite leaves: maples and sycamore have lobed leaves and paired winged fruits; horse-chestnut has hand-like compound leaves and conkers.

families.name: Urticaceae
families.tip: Small green flowers in dangling tassels; stinging nettle has stinging hairs, pellitory-of-the-wall does not.

families.name: Lycopodiaceae
families.tip: No flowers; creeping or upright stems densely covered in small, narrow, overlapping leaves; spores in cones or leaf bases.

families.name: Grossulariaceae
families.tip: Shrubs with lobed, maple-like leaves and hanging sprays of small flowers, then berries (currants, gooseberry, which is spiny).

families.name: Cistaceae
families.tip: Low, often woody-based plants of dry grassland with crumpled, short-lived yellow petals and many stamens.

families.name: Haloragaceae
families.tip: Submerged water plants with feathery leaves in whorls; small flowers on spikes above the water.

families.name: Linaceae
families.tip: Slender plants with narrow, untoothed leaves and 5 separate petals that drop quickly (fairy flax is white, flax blue).

families.name: Cornaceae
families.tip: Opposite leaves whose veins curve round towards the tip; 4-petalled flowers in flat clusters; dogwood has red winter stems.

families.name: Ulmaceae
families.tip: Trees with rough, toothed leaves that are lopsided at the base; fruit a flat papery wing round a seed.

families.name: Ophioglossaceae
families.tip: Small ferns with a single leaf and a separate spore-bearing spike or branch.

families.name: Cupressaceae
families.tip: Conifers with tiny scale-like or short prickly leaves; juniper has blue-black berry-like cones.

families.name: Aristolochiaceae
families.tip: Introduced woodland plants with heart- or kidney-shaped leaves and odd tubular or cup-shaped brownish flowers.

families.name: Montiaceae
families.tip: Small, fleshy, hairless plants with 5 white or pink petals; spring-beauty has a leaf collar round the stem below the flowers.

families.name: Resedaceae
families.tip: Spikes of small yellowish flowers with deeply cut petals and many stamens (weld, wild mignonette); bare chalky ground.

families.name: Pteridaceae
families.tip: Ferns: no flowers. Maidenhair fern has black stalks and fan-shaped leaflets; parsley fern grows in upland screes.

families.name: Nymphaeaceae
families.tip: Large round floating leaves with a slit to the centre; big white or yellow flowers floating or held just above the water.

families.name: Berberidaceae
families.tip: Spiny shrubs with yellow flowers and berries; Oregon-grape has holly-like compound leaves.

families.name: Vitaceae
families.tip: Woody climbers with tendrils; Virginia-creeper has hand-like leaves that turn red; small greenish flowers, then berries.

families.name: Polygalaceae
families.tip: Small plants of grassland and heath with blue, pink or white flowers: two large petal-like side sepals and a fringed lower petal.

families.name: Balsaminaceae
families.tip: Succulent stems; hooded, spurred flowers; seed pods that explode when touched (Himalayan balsam, touch-me-not).

families.name: Acanthaceae
families.tip: Introduced: large glossy, deeply lobed leaves and tall spikes of hooded flowers under spiny purple bracts.

families.name: Droseraceae
families.tip: Small bog plants with rosettes of round or narrow leaves covered in sticky red hairs that trap insects.

families.name: Isoetaceae
families.tip: No flowers; underwater rosettes of stiff, quill-like leaves at the bottom of clear lakes; spores at the leaf bases.

families.name: Lythraceae
families.tip: Purple-loosestrife: tall spikes of magenta flowers with 6 crinkled petals by water. Water-purslane is small and creeping.

families.name: Apocynaceae
families.tip: Trailing evergreen periwinkles with glossy opposite leaves and blue flowers whose 5 petals look twisted like a propeller.

families.name: Anacardiaceae
families.tip: Introduced stag's-horn sumach: shrub with velvety shoots, long pinnate leaves that turn red, dense red fruit clusters.

families.name: Phrymaceae
families.tip: Waterside plants with opposite leaves and large yellow, two-lipped, snapdragon-like flowers, often red-spotted.

families.name: Rutaceae
families.tip: Introduced aromatic shrubs with gland-dotted leaves (Mexican orange-blossom, rue).

families.name: Rhamnaceae
families.tip: Shrubs with small greenish 4 to 5-parted flowers and black berries; buckthorn is thorny with opposite leaves, alder buckthorn is thornless.

families.name: Hymenophyllaceae
families.tip: Tiny ferns with translucent fronds one cell thick, on wet shaded rocks and tree trunks in the west.

families.name: Celastraceae
families.tip: Spindle: shrub with green stems and pink four-lobed fruits with orange seeds. Grass-of-Parnassus: white 5-petalled flowers with fringed glands, wet places.

families.name: Juglandaceae
families.tip: Introduced trees with large aromatic pinnate leaves and catkins; walnuts, wing-nuts.

families.name: Acoraceae
families.tip: Iris-like leaves that smell of tangerines when crushed; a green finger-like flower spike sticking out sideways from a leaf-like stem.

families.name: Menyanthaceae
families.tip: Water plants: bogbean has three-part leaves and fringed white-pink flowers; fringed water-lily has small round floating leaves and yellow flowers.

families.name: Dennstaedtiaceae
families.tip: Fern: no flowers. Bracken has tall, single, much-divided fronds rising from underground stems, often in large stands.

families.name: Thymelaeaceae
families.tip: Shrubs with leathery leaves crowded towards the shoot tips and scented four-lobed flowers, then poisonous berries (mezereon, spurge-laurel).

families.name: Santalaceae
families.tip: Mistletoe: evergreen ball of forked green stems in trees, white berries. Bastard-toadflax: small parasitic herb of chalk grassland.

families.name: Zosteraceae
families.tip: Marine plants: long, grass-like ribbon leaves on sandy and muddy shores below the tide line.

families.name: Myricaceae
families.tip: Low shrub of bogs with grey-green leaves that smell resinous when crushed; catkins in spring.

families.name: Elatinaceae
families.tip: Tiny creeping plants of lake edges and mud with opposite leaves and minute pinkish flowers.

families.name: Ceratophyllaceae
families.tip: Rootless submerged water plants with whorls of stiff, forked, finely toothed leaves.

families.name: Cannabaceae
families.tip: Hop: twining rough-stemmed climber with lobed leaves and papery, cone-like female flower heads.

families.name: Juncaginaceae
families.tip: Grass-like plants of salt marsh and wet ground with fleshy, narrow leaves and a long slender spike of tiny green flowers.

families.name: Elaeagnaceae
families.tip: Spiny shrub with narrow silvery leaves and bright orange berries, mostly on sand dunes.

families.name: Selaginellaceae
families.tip: Small moss-like plant with tiny pointed leaves, in wet upland grassland and flushes; no flowers.

families.name: Pittosporaceae
families.tip: Introduced evergreen shrubs or trees with glossy leaves and small dark purple scented flowers; south-west coasts.

families.name: Ruppiaceae
families.tip: Submerged plants of brackish pools with thread-like leaves; flowers on long stalks.

families.name: Myrtaceae
families.tip: Introduced evergreen shrubs with aromatic, gland-dotted opposite leaves, white flowers with many stamens and edible berries.

families.name: Nothofagaceae
families.tip: Introduced trees planted for forestry, similar to beech but with smaller leaves.

families.name: Verbenaceae
families.tip: Wiry plant with square stems, lobed opposite leaves and long thin spikes of tiny lilac flowers.

families.name: Sarraceniaceae
families.tip: Introduced to a few bogs: leaves form upright tubes (pitchers) that trap insects.

families.name: Aquifoliaceae
families.tip: Evergreen tree or shrub with glossy, usually spiny leaves, small white 4-petalled flowers and red berries.

families.name: Alstroemeriaceae
families.tip: Garden escape with twisted leaf stalks and showy streaked flowers with 6 tepals.

families.name: Melanthiaceae
families.tip: Woodland plant with a single ring of four broad leaves and one starry green flower, then a black berry.

families.name: Marsileaceae
families.tip: Tiny fern of pond margins with grass-like leaves that uncurl like a crozier and pea-sized spore pills at the base.

families.name: Limnanthaceae
families.tip: Garden escape (poached-egg plant): white petals with yellow centres and divided leaves.

families.name: Lauraceae
families.tip: Bay: evergreen tree or shrub with aromatic leathery leaves used in cooking.

families.name: Frankeniaceae
families.tip: Low, mat-forming plant of salt marshes with tiny inrolled leaves and small pink flowers.

families.name: Eriocaulaceae
families.tip: Western Scottish and Irish lakes: underwater rosettes of grass-like leaves and small white button-heads on leafless stalks above the water.

families.name: Gunneraceae
families.tip: Introduced: gigantic rhubarb-like leaves on prickly stalks, with a huge cone-like spike of tiny flowers.

families.name: Butomaceae
families.tip: Tall water-edge plant with three-angled leaves and an umbel of pink six-petalled flowers.

families.name: Cabombaceae
families.tip: Introduced aquarium plant: submerged fan-shaped, finely divided opposite leaves and small white flowers.

families.name: Buxaceae
families.tip: Evergreen shrub with small, glossy, oval opposite leaves and tiny greenish flowers; chalk slopes and gardens.

families.name: Calceolariaceae
families.tip: Introduced: pouched, slipper-shaped yellow two-lipped flowers.

families.name: Colchicaceae
families.tip: Pink crocus-like flowers in autumn without leaves; broad leaves appear in spring. Poisonous.

families.name: Cucurbitaceae
families.tip: Climber with coiled tendrils, rough lobed leaves, greenish-white flowers and red berries.

families.name: Diapensiaceae
families.tip: Very rare: cushion plant on one Scottish mountain, with white five-petalled flowers.

families.name: Dioscoreaceae
families.tip: Twining climber with glossy heart-shaped leaves, small greenish flowers and red berries; no tendrils.

families.name: Pontederiaceae
families.tip: Introduced water plants with glossy leaves and spikes of blue flowers.

families.name: Portulacaceae
families.tip: Fleshy, sprawling annual with small yellow flowers; a garden weed.

families.name: Polemoniaceae
families.tip: Ladder-like pinnate leaves and clusters of blue bell-shaped flowers; limestone in northern England.

families.name: Paulowniaceae
families.tip: Introduced tree with very large, soft, opposite leaves and upright clusters of violet foxglove-like flowers.

families.name: Phytolaccaceae
families.tip: Introduced tall plant with reddish stems, upright spikes of small flowers and dark purple berries.

families.name: Moraceae
families.tip: Introduced tree with heart-shaped, sometimes lobed leaves, milky sap and blackberry-like fruits.

families.name: Osmundaceae
families.tip: Large fern of wet places whose fertile fronds end in rusty-brown, flower-like spore clusters; no true flowers.

families.name: Paeoniaceae
families.tip: Garden escape with large red flowers and divided leaves.

families.name: Nartheciaceae
families.tip: Bog plant with flat, sword-shaped leaves and spikes of starry orange-yellow flowers.

families.name: Scheuchzeriaceae
families.tip: Very rare bog plant with grass-like leaves that have a pore at the tip, and a few yellowish-green flowers.

families.name: Salviniaceae
families.tip: Introduced tiny floating fern forming red or green carpets on still water; no flowers.

families.name: Saururaceae
families.tip: Introduced: heart-shaped leaves smelling of orange peel and spikes of tiny flowers with four white petal-like bracts.

families.name: Tropaeolaceae
families.tip: Garden escape with round, umbrella-like leaves and orange or yellow spurred flowers.

families.name: Tofieldiaceae
families.tip: Small northern plant of wet flushes with a fan of short flat leaves and a tight head of pale greenish-white flowers.

families.name: Simaroubaceae
families.tip: Introduced tree with very long pinnate leaves, unpleasant-smelling when crushed, and twisted winged fruits.

families.name: Cyatheaceae
families.tip: Introduced tree-fern (Dicksonia) with a fibrous trunk topped by large fronds; south-west gardens and woods.

families.name: Taxaceae
families.tip: Evergreen conifer with flat, dark green needles in two rows and red fleshy cups around single seeds; no cones. All parts except the red flesh are poisonous.

species.name: Acer campestre
species.tip: Small tree or hedge maple with small, three- to five-lobed rounded leaves and corky-ridged twigs; upright green flower clusters; fruits have horizontally spread wings.

species.name: Acer platanoides
species.tip: Maple with sharply pointed lobes and bright yellow-green flower clusters appearing before the leaves in spring; milky sap in the leaf stalk and widely spread fruit wings.

species.name: Acer pseudoplatanus
species.tip: Large tree with big, five-lobed, coarsely toothed leaves and hanging spikes of yellow-green flowers; paired winged fruits spread at a narrow angle.

species.name: Achillea millefolium
species.tip: Flat-topped clusters of tiny white or pinkish daisies over feathery, finely divided dark green leaves with an aromatic smell. Common in grassland and verges, summer to autumn.

species.name: Achillea ptarmica
species.tip: Like yarrow but with undivided, narrow, sharply saw-edged leaves and fewer, larger creamy white heads with a greenish centre. Damp meadows, rushy pastures and moorland edges.

species.name: Aconitum napellus
species.tip: Tall spikes of deep blue-violet hooded flowers; deeply cut hand-shaped leaves; shady streamsides. Very poisonous.

species.name: Actaea spicata
species.tip: Rare, in limestone woods and pavement in northern England; fluffy spikes of small white flowers, then black berries.

species.name: Adonis annua
species.tip: Rare cornfield annual with feathery leaves and blood-red flowers with a dark centre.

species.name: Adoxa moschatellina
species.tip: Tiny green-yellow flowers clustered in a cube-shaped head of five, four facing sideways and one up; woodland, spring, smells musky.

species.name: Aegopodium podagraria
species.tip: Spreading patch-forming plant of shady gardens and waste ground with leaves in threes of three toothed leaflets; flat white umbels, no bristles on fruit, lacks the tall stature of hogweed.

species.name: Aesculus carnea
species.tip: Planted tree like Horse-chestnut but with deep pink-red flowers in candles, dark leaflets and smoother fruits lacking strong spines.

species.name: Aesculus hippocastanum
species.tip: Large tree with big hand-shaped leaves of five to seven leaflets, sticky buds and upright candles of white flowers spotted red or yellow; spiky conkers.

species.name: Aethusa cynapium
species.tip: Weed of cultivated ground with glossy, dark, finely cut leaves; the key clue is the long thread-like bracteoles hanging down beneath each small umbel, unlike Cow Parsley.

species.name: Agrimonia eupatoria
species.tip: Tall spike of small yellow flowers with hooked burrs; fruit grooved to the base, leaves lacking lemon scent; dry grassland and verges. Compare Fragrant Agrimony

species.name: Agrimonia procera
species.tip: Taller and coarser than Agrimony, scented when crushed; fruit bell-shaped with spreading lower bristles, grooves only part way; favours shady hedge banks and woodland edges.

species.name: Agrostemma githago
species.tip: Tall slender plant with silky grey hairs and large purple-pink flowers with long narrow sepals extending beyond the petals. Now rare cornfield annual, occasional from seed mixes.

species.name: Agrostis canina
species.tip: Fine, tufted bent of acid grassland with a long pointed ligule and a bent awn on the lemma; spreads by leafy runners and heads contract after flowering.

species.name: Agrostis capillaris
species.tip: Very common lawn and grassland bent with a short, blunt ligule and an open airy panicle; rarely awned and slightly spreading by rhizomes.

species.name: Agrostis gigantea
species.tip: Tall, creeping bent with a long, blunt ligule and rough leaves; panicle stays open and reddish, mainly on arable margins and rough ground.

species.name: Agrostis stolonifera
species.tip: Mat-forming bent with long leafy runners and a long ligule; panicle contracts into a narrow lobed shape after flowering, in damp ground and lawns.

species.name: Agrostis vinealis
species.tip: Tufted bent of dry acid heath with a longer ligule than Common Bent and a small awn; short rhizomes and a narrow brownish panicle.

species.name: Aira caryophyllea
species.tip: Tiny annual of dry sandy ground with an airy silvery-purple panicle on hair-thin branches; spikelets bear a bent awn and the ligule is long.

species.name: Aira praecox
species.tip: Small annual with a dense, short, spike-like panicle, shiny and yellowish-green; flowers very early on dry sandy soil, with bristly hair-like leaves.

species.name: Ajuga reptans
species.tip: Glossy leaves, leafy runners and a very short upper lip.

species.name: Alcea rosea
species.tip: Very tall garden plant self-seeding on walls and pavements, with large, funnel-shaped flowers in many colours on stout hairy spikes and big rounded, lobed leaves.

species.name: Alchemilla filicaulis
species.tip: One of the lady's-mantle microspecies, a specialist group; leaves hairy, stems with downward-pressed hairs; yellow-green flowers without petals; grassland and verges, mainly north and west.

species.name: Alchemilla glabra
species.tip: Lady's-mantle with leaves and stems hairless, rounded lobes with teeth; upland grassland, rock ledges and roadsides in the north and west. Specialist group; check with a specialist.

species.name: Alchemilla mollis
species.tip: Large garden plant with soft velvety hairy leaves and big frothy yellow-green flower sprays; escapes onto roadsides and waste ground. Native lady's-mantles are smaller and less downy.

species.name: Alchemilla xanthochlora
species.tip: Lady's-mantle with leaves mostly hairless above but hairy beneath on veins, stems hairy low down; damp grassland, verges and woods. Part of a specialist microspecies group.

species.name: Alisma plantago-aquatica
species.tip: Tall hairless pond-edge plant with oval basal leaves and large branched pyramidal clusters of small three-petalled pale pink-white flowers. Ponds, canals and ditches.

species.name: Alliaria petiolata
species.tip: Hedgerow and woodland-edge plant with heart-shaped toothed leaves that smell of garlic when crushed, and small white four-petalled flowers in spring.

species.name: Allium paradoxum
species.tip: Spring white drooping umbel with few flowers and bulbils among them; flat, broad, keeled leaves smelling of garlic; a garden escape on verges and hedgebanks, unlike Three-cornered Garlic.

species.name: Allium triquetrum
species.tip: Sharply three-angled flower stem and drooping one-sided cluster of white bells with green stripes; a garden escape on banks and verges, mostly in the south and west.

species.name: Allium ursinum
species.tip: Carpets damp woods with strong garlic smell; broad oval stalked leaves and a rounded umbel of star-like white flowers distinguish it from other wild garlics.

species.name: Allium vineale
species.tip: Slender hollow cylindrical leaves and a pinkish-green head often with bulbils and long-beaked spathe; grassy places and verges in summer, unlike the white-flowered garlics.

species.name: Alnus cordata
species.tip: Planted tree with glossy, heart-shaped leaves and cone-like fruits; rounder leaves than Alder; catkins appear in late winter.

species.name: Alnus glutinosa
species.tip: Wet-ground tree with rounded leaves with a notched tip, small woody cone-like fruits and purple-brown male catkins in late winter.

species.name: Alnus incana
species.tip: Tree with pointed grey-green oval leaves, downy beneath, and catkins in winter; leaves sharper than Alder, with no notch at the tip.

species.name: Alopecurus geniculatus
species.tip: Bristly cylindrical head with awns, found in wet ground; stems bend at the nodes and root there, and the anthers are orange, unlike Meadow Foxtail.

species.name: Alopecurus myosuroides
species.tip: Arable weed with a slender, tapering, often purplish cylindrical head; awned like other foxtails, but annual and lacking the soft downy feel of Meadow Foxtail.

species.name: Alopecurus pratensis
species.tip: Soft, pale cylindrical head resembling Timothy but with a bristle on each spikelet; flowers early in spring in meadows, with a long ligule.

species.name: Amsinckia micrantha
species.tip: Rough bristly annual with one-sided coiled spikes of tiny yellow flowers. Alien weed of arable land, waste ground and sandy places.

species.name: Anacamptis pyramidalis
species.tip: Orchid of chalk and limestone grassland with a dense, conical, bright pink flower head that turns dome-like; long spur on each flower and unspotted narrow leaves.

species.name: Anemone apennina
species.tip: Garden escape like Wood Anemone but with sky-blue flowers of 10 to 15 narrow petals.

species.name: Anemone blanda
species.tip: Garden escape; low plant with many narrow blue, pink or white petals in early spring.

species.name: Anemone nemorosa
species.tip: Spring carpets in old woods; a single white flower, often pink-tinged beneath, above a ring of three divided leaves.

species.name: Angelica sylvestris
species.tip: Tall plant of damp meadows and woods with purplish stems and rounded, pinkish-tinged umbels; leaf stalks sheath the stem with inflated bases, unlike Hogweed.

species.name: Anisantha diandra
species.tip: Large drooping panicle with very long awns on big spikelets; sheaths softly hairy; spikelets longer than Barren Brome with branches rarely over 5 cm.

species.name: Anisantha sterilis
species.tip: Common roadside annual with a drooping panicle of long-awned spikelets spreading to one side; hairy sheaths and branches longer than Great Brome.

species.name: Antennaria dioica
species.tip: Low mat with white woolly spoon-shaped leaves and short stalks of papery pink or white button heads that never open as daisies. Upland grassland and heath.

species.name: Anthoxanthum odoratum
species.tip: Smells of new-mown hay when crushed; spike-like yellowish-green head, early flowering, with a short awn on the lower lemmas and slightly hairy leaves.

species.name: Anthriscus caucalis
species.tip: Small annual of hedge banks and waste ground with tiny umbels of few rays and spiny-bristled fruits; flowers earlier and is smaller than Upright Hedge-parsley.

species.name: Anthriscus sylvestris
species.tip: Early-flowering roadside and hedgerow umbellifer with fine fern-like leaves and smooth, ridged, hollow stems; flowers April to June, well before Hogweed or Hemlock.

species.name: Anthyllis vulneraria
species.tip: Round heads of yellow, sometimes orange or red, flowers cupped by furry bracts, with silky pinnate leaves; grassland, cliffs and dunes.

species.name: Antirrhinum majus
species.tip: Garden escape on old walls and rubbly ground; large two-lipped flowers closed by a pouting lower lip, unlike the toadflaxes with spurs. Colours vary from pink to white or yellow.

species.name: Aphanes arvensis
species.tip: Tiny low, greyish, hairy annual with fan-shaped three-lobed leaves and minute greenish flowers hidden in leaf axils; arable and dry bare ground. Separate from Slender Parsley-piert by larger fruit.

species.name: Aphanes australis
species.tip: Tiny annual like Parsley-piert but fruit smaller, sepal tube narrower and more cylindrical; acid sandy soils, arable and bare ground. Needs a lens to separate.

species.name: Aquilegia vulgaris
species.tip: Nodding flowers with five hooked spurs, usually violet-blue; leaves divided into rounded, lobed leaflets.

species.name: Arabidopsis thaliana
species.tip: Tiny annual of dry bare ground and walls with a flat rosette of small leaves and a wiry stem of tiny white flowers and long thin pods.

species.name: Arabis hirsuta
species.tip: Upright, hairy plant of dry banks and walls with clasping stem leaves pressed to the stem and small white flowers; pods held upright and close.

species.name: Arctium lappa
species.tip: Large burdock with big heart-shaped leaves and long-stalked heads in a loose flat-topped cluster; bracts have hooked tips. Told from Lesser Burdock by larger heads and solid leaf stalks.

species.name: Arctium minus
species.tip: Burdock with stalkless or short-stalked heads in a spike-like arrangement, smaller than Greater Burdock, and hooked bracts that cling to clothing. Hollow leaf stalks; waste ground and hedgerows.

species.name: Arctium nemorosum
species.tip: Burdock with heads on long stalks and bracts whose hooks are purple-tinged, mostly in woodland edges and shady verges. Heads often smaller and more open than Greater Burdock; tricky to separate.

species.name: Arenaria leptoclados
species.tip: Slender annual like Thyme-leaved Sandwort but with a longer, narrower capsule and smaller seeds; found on dry open ground and walls. Best told by a lens.

species.name: Arenaria serpyllifolia
species.tip: Wiry, much-branched annual with small hairy oval pointed leaves and tiny white flowers with petals shorter than sepals. Common on dry bare ground, walls and sandy soil.

species.name: Armeria maritima
species.tip: Cushion-forming plant of cliffs, saltmarsh and mountains with dense tufts of narrow grassy leaves and round heads of pink flowers on leafless stalks.

species.name: Armoracia rusticana
species.tip: Tall, coarse plant of roadsides and waste ground with huge dock-like basal leaves, narrower lobed upper leaves and clusters of small white flowers.

species.name: Arrhenatherum elatius
species.tip: Tall tufted grass of verges with a long open panicle of shining spikelets, each with a bent awn; stem bases often swollen like beads.

species.name: Artemisia vulgaris
species.tip: Tall, tough plant with dark green deeply cut leaves that are silvery-white beneath, and long spikes of small dull reddish-brown button heads. Waste ground, verges, late summer.

species.name: Arum italicum
species.tip: Arum with arrow-shaped leaves with pale veins appearing in autumn, and a yellow spadix; leaf lobes spread apart. Unlike native Lords-and-ladies, it is in leaf in winter.

species.name: Arum maculatum
species.tip: Woodland and hedgerow arum with arrow-shaped leaves, sometimes spotted purple, and a hooded green spathe round a purple or yellow spadix; spikes of orange-red berries in autumn.

species.name: Asplenium adiantum-nigrum
species.tip: Evergreen fern of walls, rocks and hedge banks with glossy dark triangular, twice-cut fronds on a shiny blackish stalk; lacks the green stalk of other spleenworts.

species.name: Asplenium ceterach
species.tip: Small fern of limestone walls and rocks with leathery lobed fronds densely covered beneath with overlapping rusty brown scales; may shrivel in drought and revive after rain.

species.name: Asplenium ruta-muraria
species.tip: Tiny tufted fern of limestone walls and mortar with dark green, stiff, wedge-shaped, toothed leaflets on a short stalk; leaflets resemble those of rue.

species.name: Asplenium scolopendrium
species.tip: Fern with undivided, glossy, strap-shaped fronds with wavy edge and rows of brown spore lines underneath; common in shady lanes, walls and wood banks.

species.name: Asplenium trichomanes
species.tip: Small evergreen fern of walls and rocks with narrow once-cut fronds, tiny oval leaflets along a glossy black stalk; leaflets are regular and green.

species.name: Athyrium filix-femina
species.tip: Large, delicate, lime-green fern of damp woods, with twice-cut fronds forming a shuttlecock; the spore patches are curved or hooked and the stalk base is scaly.

species.name: Atriplex glabriuscula
species.tip: Fleshy prostrate coastal orache with triangular leaves, spreading and mealy; found on shingle and strandlines, with fruiting bracts joined at base.

species.name: Atriplex littoralis
species.tip: Narrow, linear toothed leaves; upright, mainly in saltmarsh and coastal edges, differs from other oraches in narrow leaves.

species.name: Atriplex patula
species.tip: Arable weed with leaves narrowly triangular with basal lobes and fruiting bracts stalkless, toothed; stem stripes green and red; waste land.

species.name: Atriplex prostrata
species.tip: Leaves triangular with spreading basal lobes, silvery-mealy when young, often on saltmarshes and disturbed ground; fruiting bracts often stalked.

species.name: Aubrieta deltoidea
species.tip: Low mat-forming garden escape on walls and rocks with grey-green leaves and bright purple to lilac four-petalled flowers in spring.

species.name: Avena fatua
species.tip: Tall arable weed with large drooping oat spikelets, awned with a bent awn and a hairy base; spikelets fall whole and the ligule is long.

species.name: Avena sativa
species.tip: Cultivated cereal with large drooping spikelets, mostly awnless or with weak awns, unlike Wild-oat; spikelets do not shed readily.

species.name: Avenella flexuosa
species.tip: Tufted grass of heaths and acid woods with hair-fine wiry leaves and shiny purplish-bronze panicle; each spikelet has a bent awn.

species.name: Avenula pubescens
species.tip: Chalk grassland oat-grass with softly hairy leaves and sheaths, and large spikelets with a bent awn; ligule long and the panicle narrow.

species.name: Azolla filiculoides
species.tip: Tiny floating fern forming a red or green mat of overlapping scale-like leaves on still water; introduced, often turning red in autumn.

species.name: Ballota nigra
species.tip: Rank-smelling hedgerow plant; the calyx has broad, spreading teeth.

species.name: Barbarea intermedia
species.tip: Yellow-flowered winter-cress with smaller flowers than Winter-cress and slender pods; upper leaves are lobed, and the flower buds are not compact.

species.name: Barbarea vulgaris
species.tip: Shiny dark green leaves with a large rounded end lobe and smaller side lobes; yellow flowers with buds in a dense head, on damp ground and verges.

species.name: Bellis perennis
species.tip: Familiar lawn plant with a flat rosette of spoon-shaped leaves and single white-rayed, yellow-centred heads on leafless stalks. Flowers nearly all year.

species.name: Berberis vulgaris
species.tip: Spiny shrub with three-pronged spines and clusters of small leaves; hanging yellow flower sprays in May and red berries; hedgerows, unlike evergreen Oregon-grape.

species.name: Berula erecta
species.tip: Wet-ground plant of ditches and stream margins with once-pinnate glossy leaves of many toothed leaflets, and leaf-like bracts under the umbels; hairless and creeping at base.

species.name: Beta vulgaris
species.tip: Glossy dark green fleshy leaves, coastal; tall flower spikes with green flowers, shingle and sea walls, wild ancestor of beetroot.

species.name: Betonica officinalis
species.tip: Rosette of long-stalked, oblong leaves; reddish-purple flowers in a dense spike.

species.name: Betula pendula
species.tip: White papery bark with black diamond marks, hairless twigs and drooping branches; leaves double-toothed and triangular.

species.name: Betula pubescens
species.tip: Birch with hairy young twigs, whiter bark without deep fissures and oval leaves with rounded base; wet heaths and moorland.

species.name: Bidens cernua
species.tip: Yellow heads nodding on the stem, often without rays, over unlobed toothed opposite leaves. Wet margins of ponds and ditches, late summer; seeds have barbed bristles.

species.name: Bidens tripartita
species.tip: Opposite leaves usually cut into three lobes, and upright, rayless dull yellow heads with leafy bracts. Pond edges and ditches; barbed seeds stick to clothing.

species.name: Bistorta officinalis
species.tip: Dense pink poker-like spikes on unbranched stems above broad, triangular-based leaves with winged stalks; damp meadows, often in patches.

species.name: Bistorta vivipara
species.tip: Upland grassland; slender spike of white or pale pink flowers, the lower part replaced by small purplish bulbils; narrow leaves.

species.name: Blackstonia perfoliata
species.tip: Blue-grey plant of chalk and limestone grassland with paired leaves fused around the stem and bright yellow flowers having eight petals that close in dull weather.

species.name: Blechnum spicant
species.tip: Fern of acid woods and heaths with two types of frond: sterile ones are glossy, once-cut and in a flat rosette, while fertile ones are upright and narrow.

species.name: Blitum bonus-henricus
species.tip: Farmyards and roadsides; mealy, broad triangular arrow-shaped leaves and tall leafless spikes of tiny greenish flowers.

species.name: Bolboschoenus maritimus
species.tip: Tall triangular-stemmed plant of brackish marshes and estuaries with a tight clump of chestnut-brown spikelets and long leafy bracts overtopping the head; leaves flat, keeled and rough-edged.

species.name: Borago officinalis
species.tip: Bristly plant with bright blue starry flowers having a dark central cone. Garden escape on tips and waste ground; unlike other blue borages by its star shape.

species.name: Botrychium lunaria
species.tip: Small fern with a single half-moon shaped pinnae on a fleshy frond and a separate spore spike; short turf, dunes and grassland, often hard to spot.

species.name: Brachypodium sylvaticum
species.tip: Shade-loving, yellowish-green, drooping spike of short-stalked awned spikelets in woods and hedges; leaves broad, softly hairy and flopping.

species.name: Brassica napus
species.tip: Blue-grey hairless leaves whose upper ones clasp the stem; open flowers sit level with or just above the buds in crop fields and verges.

species.name: Brassica nigra
species.tip: Tall, bristly plant of riverbanks and coasts with small yellow flowers and short pods pressed tight against the stem; lower leaves lobed and rough.

species.name: Brassica rapa
species.tip: Upper leaves clasp the stem with rounded basal lobes, grey-green and slightly waxy, and open flowers overtop the buds; found by rivers and on waste ground.

species.name: Briza media
species.tip: Chalk grassland grass with heart-shaped, trembling, purplish spikelets hanging on hair-fine stalks in a loose open panicle; no awns.

species.name: Bromopsis erecta
species.tip: Chalk grassland brome with erect panicle and stiff erect branches, awned spikelets, and rolled leaves with hairs on the margins and sheaths.

species.name: Bromopsis ramosa
species.tip: Woodland brome with a drooping panicle of few long-awned spikelets and broad, hairy leaves; the sheaths bristle with spreading hairs.

species.name: Bromus hordeaceus
species.tip: Common brome with a short, dense, erect, softly downy panicle; leaves and sheaths soft with hairs, and spikelets bear short straight awns.

species.name: Bromus racemosus
species.tip: Brome of damp meadows with an erect panicle of smooth spikelets, shorter awns than Rye Brome and sheaths often hairy; spikelets not downy.

species.name: Bromus secalinus
species.tip: Annual weed of cornfields with nodding spikelets that have short, outcurved awns; spikelets are swollen and plump, becoming weakly twisted.

species.name: Bryonia dioica
species.tip: Climbing hedge plant with tendrils, palmately lobed rough leaves and greenish-white flowers, followed by red berries; the only British climber with tendrils in this family.

species.name: Buddleja davidii
species.tip: Shrub of walls, railways and waste ground with long, arching cones of fragrant lilac-purple flowers, narrow pointed leaves white-felted beneath, loved by butterflies.

species.name: Butomus umbellatus
species.tip: Tall plant of water margins with narrow triangular leaves and umbels of pink flowers on a tall stem; not a rush, summer.

species.name: Buxus sempervirens
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with small opposite glossy oval leaves; tiny greenish-yellow flowers in clusters in spring; native on chalk slopes, widely planted in hedges.

species.name: Cakile maritima
species.tip: Fleshy, lobed-leaved plant of sandy and shingle beaches with pale lilac to white flowers and short, swollen, two-segmented pods.

species.name: Calamagrostis epigejos
species.tip: Tall, creeping, tough grass with a dense, purplish-brown plume and a hairy-based bristle on each floret; leaves rough and stiff, on scrub and rough ground.

species.name: Calendula officinalis
species.tip: Garden escape with bright orange or yellow large daisy heads, rather fleshy aromatic sticky leaves and curved ridged seeds. Found on tips, waste ground and field edges.

species.name: Callitriche brutia
species.tip: Tiny aquatic or mud-dwelling plant with starry leaf rosettes; fruits sit on distinct stalks, unlike other water-starworts whose fruits are stalkless. Often on seasonally drying pools and ditches.

species.name: Callitriche platycarpa
species.tip: Water-starwort with floating rosettes of rounded leaves; fruits are stalkless and winged at the top, with spreading styles. Common in ponds and ditches, often with Common Water-starwort.

species.name: Callitriche stagnalis
species.tip: Most frequent water-starwort; floating rosettes of broad rounded leaves and stalkless fruits that are broadly winged, with a clearly keeled edge. Ponds, ditches and wet mud.

species.name: Calluna vulgaris
species.tip: Tiny scale-like leaves pressed along the stem and small pale pink-purple bells with a prominent calyx; common on moors and heaths, later than the other heaths.

species.name: Caltha palustris
species.tip: Large glossy kidney-shaped leaves; big golden cup flowers with no green sepals beneath; marshes and wet woods.

species.name: Calystegia pulchra
species.tip: Climber with large pink flowers, often with white stripes, and hairy stems; bracts under the flower do not overlap the sepals, and stems often hairy, unlike Hedge Bindweed.

species.name: Calystegia sepium
species.tip: Twining climber of hedges and wasteland with large white trumpets, arrow-shaped leaves, and bracteoles that are small and do not hide the sepals; hairless stems.

species.name: Calystegia silvatica
species.tip: Vigorous garden escape with large white or pink-flushed trumpets whose big bracts overlap and swell around the base of the flower; leaves broadly arrow-shaped.

species.name: Campanula latifolia
species.tip: Tall leafy plant with large blue-purple bells in a leafy spike; stem rounded and hairy, leaves coarse and pointed; shady woods, north England and Scotland.

species.name: Campanula persicifolia
species.tip: Wide open bowl-shaped blue flowers on a slender stem with narrow, shiny, finely toothed leaves; a garden escape on banks and verges.

species.name: Campanula portenschlagiana
species.tip: Mat-forming wall plant with dense violet star-shaped bells, deeply five-lobed, and small rounded toothed leaves; garden escape on walls and pavements.

species.name: Campanula poscharskyana
species.tip: Sprawling plant with pale lilac starry flowers cut nearly to the base and heart-shaped toothed leaves; naturalised on walls and banks.

species.name: Campanula rotundifolia
species.tip: Slender nodding pale blue bells on wiry stems; basal leaves rounded, stem leaves very narrow; grassland and dunes, late summer.

species.name: Campanula trachelium
species.tip: Tall, roughly hairy, angular stem with nettle-like coarse toothed leaves and large blue-purple bells; woods and hedgerows, mainly lowland England and Wales.

species.name: Capsella bursa-pastoris
species.tip: Common weed with tiny white flowers and flat heart-shaped or triangular pods like little purses; basal rosette of variably lobed leaves.

species.name: Cardamine amara
species.tip: Damp-ground bitter-cress with white flowers and distinctive purple anthers; stem is solid and leafy, with large flowers for the group.

species.name: Cardamine flexuosa
species.tip: Zigzag hairy stem with leaves on it; usually six stamens and a rosette of leaves; shady, damp ground and gardens, often taller than Hairy Bitter-cress.

species.name: Cardamine hirsuta
species.tip: Small annual weed of bare ground with a rosette of pinnate leaves and few stem leaves; usually four stamens; pods shoot out when ripe.

species.name: Cardamine pratensis
species.tip: Pale lilac or pink flowers in damp meadows in spring; pinnate leaves with rounded leaflets on lower stem, narrow ones above; also called Lady's Smock.

species.name: Carduus crispus
species.tip: Slender thistle whose stems are winged right up to the heads with wavy spiny wings, and small clustered purple heads. Verges and rough grass in summer.

species.name: Carduus nutans
species.tip: Big nodding purple heads with broad spreading spiny bracts, and spiny-winged stems below. Grows on chalk and limestone grassland and disturbed ground, summer.

species.name: Carex acutiformis
species.tip: Blue-green broad leaves with a ligule that is long and pointed; two or three thick male spikes above, stout upright females below with pointed utricles; wet ground and ditches.

species.name: Carex arenaria
species.tip: Found on coastal dunes, with long creeping runners that send up stems in a straight line; spikes in a loose brownish cluster, each with male flowers on top and female below.

species.name: Carex binervis
species.tip: Moorland and heath sedge with a single male spike above and spaced, stalked, upright to slightly nodding female spikes; leaves greyish-green and utricles with two clear green ribs.

species.name: Carex canescens
species.tip: Small grey-green tufts in wet acid places, with several rounded, pale spikes spaced along the stem, each with female flowers above male; utricles pale and small.

species.name: Carex caryophyllea
species.tip: Low early-flowering sedge of dry grassland and limestone with one male spike and short downy-fruited female spikes; base of stems has reddish-purple sheaths; leaves short and soft.

species.name: Carex dioica
species.tip: Tiny single-spiked sedge of base-rich flushes and fens, with male and female spikes on separate plants; stems slender, leaves narrow, spreading by short runners.

species.name: Carex distans
species.tip: Coastal and brackish sedge with bluish-green leaves and a short ligule; female spikes widely spaced, small, held close to the stem, with a long-beaked yellowish-green utricle.

species.name: Carex disticha
species.tip: Wet meadow and fen sedge with long creeping runners; the spike is a dense brown cylinder of stacked small spikelets, male flowers in the middle and female at both ends.

species.name: Carex divulsa
species.tip: Greyish-green sedge of hedgebanks, with a long interrupted head of small spikes, lower ones well spaced, each with male above female; utricles brownish-green with a long beak.

species.name: Carex echinata
species.tip: Small yellowish-green sedge of wet acid ground whose few spikes cluster together and fruits spread out starlike when ripe; spikes show male above female within each.

species.name: Carex flacca
species.tip: Leaves distinctly blue-grey beneath, and stiff on chalk and limestone; blackish-purple male spikes with a short nodding female spike lower down; runs by rhizomes.

species.name: Carex hirta
species.tip: Leaves, sheaths and fruits all bear obvious hairs; creeping plant of rough grassland and ditches with widely spaced female spikes below two or three male spikes.

species.name: Carex hostiana
species.tip: Yellowish-tawny sedge of fens and flushes; compact female spikes are clustered near the male spike, each fruit with a bent-back short beak; leaves flat and rather pale.

species.name: Carex laevigata
species.tip: Broad, shiny, bright green leaves with smooth edges in damp woods; slender female spikes slightly nodding, widely spaced, on smooth stems, with a pale winged utricle.

species.name: Carex leporina
species.tip: A tight oval cluster of pale straw-coloured spikes at stem top, each with male flowers above female; damp grassland and rushy pastures; the fruit is flat and winged.

species.name: Carex muricata
species.tip: Green spikes on short compact stalks, with spreading fruit giving a prickly look; lowest spikes spaced, flowers male above female; includes similar close relatives, so check details.

species.name: Carex nigra
species.tip: Smooth blue-green leaves; one or two slender male spikes, and black-scaled narrow female spikes with short stalks in boggy and grassy places; fruit small and rounded.

species.name: Carex otrubae
species.tip: Dense, green, clustered head of spikes, often over 5 cm, with a long pointed ligule and a lower sheath that stays pale; damp grassland, ditches, often brackish.

species.name: Carex pallescens
species.tip: Pale green sedge with hairy leaves and sheaths; short egg-shaped female spikes hang on thin stalks below a single male spike; woods and grassland.

species.name: Carex panicea
species.tip: Waxy blue-green leaves like carnation foliage; one male spike and widely spaced female spikes with plump, rounded fruits bearing a short beak; damp meadows and fens.

species.name: Carex paniculata
species.tip: Forms large tussocks in fens and carr; branched, plume-like head of many small spikes, male and female mingled; stem sharply triangular and rough; leaves stiff.

species.name: Carex pendula
species.tip: Big tufted sedge with long, thick, drooping female spikes up to 16 cm hanging on slender stalks; leaves broad and shiny; woods and damp shady banks.

species.name: Carex pilulifera
species.tip: Small tufted heath sedge with round, hairy-fruited female spikes clustered tight at the base of the male spike, like little pills; leaves are soft and slender.

species.name: Carex pseudocyperus
species.tip: Yellow-green leaves and long hanging female spikes with fruits bearing long, spreading awns; edge of ponds and slow water; looks like Pendulous Sedge but spikes thinner.

species.name: Carex pulicaris
species.tip: Small wiry tufted sedge of damp base-rich ground with one small spike, male flowers above and shiny dark brown fruits below that curve down like fleas.

species.name: Carex remota
species.tip: Soft, thin, pale green leaves in shady damp woods and ditches; small green spikes well separated up the stem, with long leafy bracts below them; fruit tiny.

species.name: Carex riparia
species.tip: Big grey-green creeping sedge of pond edges with three to five thick male spikes and long upright females; leaves broad, rough-edged; the ligule is blunt.

species.name: Carex rostrata
species.tip: Bluish-green sedge of bogs and lake margins; yellowish female spikes with spreading bottle-shaped fruits having a long beak; leaves narrow and rolled.

species.name: Carex spicata
species.tip: Dense compact cluster of male and female spikes at the top of a sharply triangular stem; grassy verges and rough ground; fruits small, pointed and ribbed.

species.name: Carex sylvatica
species.tip: Bright green leaves and thin, long-stalked, drooping female spikes spaced up the stem; woodland sedge with fruit that is slender and beaked.

species.name: Carex vesicaria
species.tip: Swollen, inflated yellowish-green fruits spreading from stout female spikes; wet places, pond margins; leaves yellow-green with blunt ligule; paler than Bottle Sedge.

species.name: Carlina vulgaris
species.tip: Stiff, spiny, small thistle with straw-coloured, shiny bracts spreading like rays around a brown centre; dead heads persist through winter. Dry chalk and limestone grassland.

species.name: Carpinus betulus
species.tip: Tree with fluted grey trunk and oval leaves with parallel pleated veins, double-toothed; fruit has three-lobed bracts.

species.name: Castanea sativa
species.tip: Large tree with long toothed glossy leaves, long yellowish catkins and spiny husked nuts; deeply spiralled bark in older trees.

species.name: Catapodium marinum
species.tip: Stiff, short, one-sided spike of spikelets, close to the ground on rocks and sea walls; spikelets sit straight on the stem and are unawned.

species.name: Catapodium rigidum
species.tip: Small, rigid grass of dry walls and dry ground, with a triangular stiff panicle with very short branches carrying unawned spikelets.

species.name: Centaurea cyanus
species.tip: Slender grey-green plant with bright blue heads whose outer florets are large and spreading. Arable field edges, wasteland and sown wildflower strips, summer.

species.name: Centaurea debeauxii
species.tip: Slender knapweed with deeply cut stem leaves and rather small purple heads with narrow, pale-fringed bracts. Chalk grassland in southern England; hard to separate from Common Knapweed.

species.name: Centaurea montana
species.tip: Garden escape with large blue heads whose outer florets are spreading, and bracts edged with black fringes. Leaves are broad and unlobed; found on verges and waste ground.

species.name: Centaurea nigra
species.tip: Purple thistle-like heads with dark brown, comb-fringed bracts forming a rounded knob, over unlobed or slightly lobed leaves. Abundant in grassland; no spines.

species.name: Centaurea scabiosa
species.tip: Larger knapweed with deeply cut leaves and heads with black-tipped bracts that are not a dark mop; outer florets are enlarged. Dry calcareous grassland.

species.name: Centaurium erythraea
species.tip: Pink flowers with five petals and a yellow centre, in flat-topped clusters; stem leaves are oval, with a basal rosette; dry grassland, dunes and woodland rides.

species.name: Centranthus ruber
species.tip: Pink-red, occasionally white, flowers in dense clusters, each with a short spur; grey-green fleshy leaves; naturalised on old walls, cliffs and railway lines.

species.name: Cerastium diffusum
species.tip: Small coastal annual with tiny flowers, bracts leafy and bracts without membranous margins in tufts. Bears five stamens and four petals; found on sand and dunes.

species.name: Cerastium fontanum
species.tip: Perennial with hairy oval leaves, flowers with white notched petals about as long as sepals and sparse inflorescence. Common in grassland and lawns; a perennial, unlike the annual species.

species.name: Cerastium glomeratum
species.tip: Annual, sticky and hairy, with compact flower clusters of five-petalled white flowers with petals about equal to sepals. Waste ground, paths and arable fields.

species.name: Cerastium semidecandrum
species.tip: Tiny, early-flowering annual of dry sandy places with sepals having broad papery margins and petals that are small. Flowers disappear by early summer.

species.name: Cerastium tomentosum
species.tip: Garden escape forming silvery-white woolly mats with narrow leaves and masses of larger white flowers. Walls, banks and waste ground.

species.name: Ceratocapnos claviculata
species.tip: Delicate climber of acid woods and heaths using tendril-tipped leaves and clusters of tiny cream flowers; the leaves are divided into small oval leaflets.

species.name: Ceratophyllum demersum
species.tip: Submerged rootless plant with stiff dark green whorled forked leaves with tiny teeth; flowers seldom seen, in still and slow water.

species.name: Chaenorhinum minus
species.tip: Small, sticky-hairy annual of arable fields and railway ballast; tiny pale purple flowers with a short spur, much smaller than Common Toadflax and with no yellow.

species.name: Chaerophyllum temulum
species.tip: Hairy hedgerow plant with purple-spotted, bristly swollen-jointed stems; flowers later than Cow Parsley and is much coarser to the touch with rough leaves.

species.name: Chamaenerion angustifolium
species.tip: Tall stands of magenta flower spikes on waste ground, clearings and railways; long narrow leaves arranged spirally; seeds with white fluff in late summer.

species.name: Chelidonium majus
species.tip: Plant of hedge banks and walls, with brittle stems that bleed orange latex, blue-green deeply cut leaves and clusters of small four-petalled yellow flowers.

species.name: Chenopodium album
species.tip: Common weed with mealy white-dusted leaves, diamond-shaped to toothed, and dense green flower clusters; arable and waste ground.

species.name: Chenopodium ficifolium
species.tip: Leaves with three lobes, central lobe long, parallel-sided, near-hairless; arable and disturbed ground, unlike Fat-hen.

species.name: Chrysosplenium alternifolium
species.tip: Small damp-woodland plant with leaves alternate on the stem, kidney-shaped and hairy, with yellow-green bracts around tiny flowers; rarer than the opposite-leaved species.

species.name: Chrysosplenium oppositifolium
species.tip: Mat-forming plant of streamsides and wet woods with paired, rounded, fleshy leaves and flat clusters of tiny golden-green flowers amid yellowish leaf-like bracts.

species.name: Cicerbita macrophylla
species.tip: Tall hairy plant with pale blue-violet dandelion-like heads and large leaves with a big triangular end lobe. Escaped from gardens to damp shady verges and woodland edges.

species.name: Cichorium intybus
species.tip: Tall, stiff, branching plant with bright sky-blue dandelion-like heads that open in the morning, stalkless along the stems. Dry grassland, verges and field edges.

species.name: Circaea lutetiana
species.tip: Shade-loving woodland and garden weed with paired opposite oval leaves and slender spikes of tiny white flowers with only two notched petals; fruits are bristly burs.

species.name: Cirsium acaule
species.tip: Stemless thistle with a flat rosette of spiny leaves and one or more big purple heads sitting at ground level. Short chalk and limestone turf.

species.name: Cirsium arvense
species.tip: Common spreading thistle with lilac, scented heads in clusters, stems not winged and leaves spiny but only slightly cottony. Forms patches in fields and verges.

species.name: Cirsium heterophyllum
species.tip: Spineless thistle with unlobed, lance-shaped leaves white and felted beneath, clasping the stem, and a single large drooping purple head. Upland meadows and verges.

species.name: Cirsium palustre
species.tip: Tall, narrow thistle with spiny-winged stems and dense clusters of small purple heads at the top. Damp meadows, rushy pasture and heaths.

species.name: Cirsium vulgare
species.tip: Large heads on a spiny-winged stem, with fierce spear-shaped spiny leaves that are bristly above. Common on grassland and waste ground, late summer.

species.name: Claytonia perfoliata
species.tip: Annual with a round stem leaf cupping the tiny white flowers like a collar; spring weed of sandy cultivated ground and gardens, unlike the pink-flowered Pink Purslane.

species.name: Claytonia sibirica
species.tip: Succulent annual or biennial with a pair of separate stem leaves below pink, white-veined flowers; damp shady places, woods and gardens, not the single collar of Springbeauty.

species.name: Clematis vitalba
species.tip: Woody climber over hedges and scrub on chalk and limestone; creamy flowers with 4 sepals; feathery 'old man's beard' seed heads.

species.name: Clinopodium vulgare
species.tip: Flower whorls wrapped in long, bristly hairs, so they look woolly; only faintly aromatic.

species.name: Cochlearia danica
species.tip: Small coastal and inland-roadside annual with ivy-shaped stalked basal leaves and clusters of small white to lilac flowers in early spring.

species.name: Cochlearia officinalis
species.tip: Fleshy, shiny, rounded to heart-shaped leaves in salt marshes and sea cliffs, with white flowers in dense clusters and rounded pods.

species.name: Comarum palustre
species.tip: Wetland plant with dark purplish-red star-like flowers, sepals longer than petals; leaves with five or seven toothed leaflets; bogs, fens and wet margins.

species.name: Conium maculatum
species.tip: Tall, hairless, poisonous umbellifer with smooth stems blotched with purple and a mousy smell when crushed; much more finely cut and spotted than Cow Parsley or Angelica.

species.name: Conopodium majus
species.tip: Slender plant of old grassland and woodland edges whose feathery leaves are thread-like; stem leaves appear early, and a round edible tuber lies underground.

species.name: Consolida ajacis
species.tip: Garden escape; spikes of blue, pink or white flowers with one long spur; very finely divided leaves.

species.name: Convallaria majalis
species.tip: Low woodland carpeter with two broad, ribbed oval leaves per shoot and a one-sided spray of nodding, sweet-scented white bells; fruits red berries.

species.name: Convolvulus arvensis
species.tip: Trailing or climbing weed of fields and verges with small, scented pink or white funnels often striped, and small arrow-shaped leaves; bracts are tiny and far below the flower.

species.name: Cornus sanguinea
species.tip: Shrub with opposite oval leaves with curved veins, dark red autumn colour and winter twigs; white flower clusters in summer and black berries; hedges on chalk and clay.

species.name: Cornus sericea
species.tip: Suckering shrub with bright red winter stems, grown for colour and naturalised in damp ground; fruits white, unlike black berries of native Dogwood.

species.name: Cortaderia selloana
species.tip: Huge garden escape forming giant clumps with silvery-white plumes up to a metre long; leaves have razor-sharp edges, ligule is a fringe of hairs.

species.name: Corylus avellana
species.tip: Shrub with rounded, softly hairy toothed leaves; dangling yellow male catkins appear in late winter, tiny red female flowers.

species.name: Cotoneaster horizontalis
species.tip: Low shrub with fishbone-pattern branches, tiny glossy rounded leaves and pinkish-white flowers; red berries persist; escapes onto walls, rocks and dunes. Flat habit separates it from other cotoneasters.

species.name: Cotoneaster integrifolius
species.tip: Small evergreen shrub with leaves white-felted beneath, pink-tinged flowers and red fruits; spreads on limestone cliffs and rocks. Leaves smaller than Himalayan Cotoneaster.

species.name: Cotoneaster simonsii
species.tip: Upright semi-evergreen shrub with orange-red fruits and flowers pink outside; leaves hairy beneath. Common bird-sown escape on hedges and waste ground; taller than Wall Cotoneaster.

species.name: Crassula helmsii
species.tip: Invasive pond plant forming dense mats of paired, narrow, fleshy leaves; tiny four-petalled white flowers appear singly on leaf axils, often in water or on mud.

species.name: Crataegus laevigata
species.tip: Hawthorn with shallow three-lobed leaves and flowers with two or three styles and fruits with two stones; ancient woodland and old hedges, mainly lowland England.

species.name: Crataegus monogyna
species.tip: Common hedge thorn with deeply cut lobed leaves and one style per flower, one stone per haw; flowers May, white; compare shallow-lobed Midland Hawthorn.

species.name: Crepis biennis
species.tip: Tall hairy biennial with large golden heads and toothed, lobed leaves; outer bracts are bristly and the buds nod. Meadows and verges, early summer.

species.name: Crepis capillaris
species.tip: Small yellow dandelion-like heads in loose clusters, orange-red beneath, over mostly smooth leaves with arrow-shaped stem leaf bases. Lawns, walls, verges; flowers until late autumn.

species.name: Crepis paludosa
species.tip: Leafy plant of damp places with unlobed or little-lobed clasping stem leaves and orange-yellow heads, black-hairy bracts. Wet meadows and streamsides, northern and western Britain.

species.name: Crepis vesicaria
species.tip: Hairy plant with deeply cut leaves and yellow heads, outer florets orange-streaked beneath; fruits have a beak. Roadsides, walls and waste ground, mainly southern England.

species.name: Crocus tommasinianus
species.tip: Garden crocus naturalised on lawns and verges, with slender silvery-lilac flowers with pointed petals and grass-like leaves with a white stripe; flowers very early.

species.name: Crocus vernus
species.tip: Crocus naturalised in grass with large, goblet-shaped purple or white flowers with a throat that is often hairy; leaves narrow with a pale central stripe, flowering in early spring.

species.name: Cruciata laevipes
species.tip: Hairy bedstraw of grassland and hedge banks with whorls of four oval, three-veined leaves and tiny yellow honey-scented flower clusters in leaf axils.

species.name: Cupressus lawsoniana
species.tip: Planted conifer with flattened sprays of tiny scale leaves that smell of parsley when crushed, a drooping leading shoot and small round cones.

species.name: Cyclamen hederifolium
species.tip: Pink swept-back petals appearing before marbled, angular ivy-like leaves; naturalised in woods and churchyards in autumn.

species.name: Cymbalaria muralis
species.tip: Trailing plant hanging from walls with fleshy ivy-shaped leaves; small lilac flowers with a yellow patch and a short spur. Common on old walls and pavements.

species.name: Cynosurus cristatus
species.tip: Narrow stiff one-sided spike like a comb, shiny and green; a small awn on each spikelet and wiry flower stems; common in pasture.

species.name: Cyperus longus
species.tip: Rare tall plant of wet places with a spreading umbel of reddish-brown flat spikelets and long leafy bracts; stem triangular; unlike a sedge, no sac-like fruits.

species.name: Cystopteris fragilis
species.tip: Small delicate fern of walls, rock crevices and mountains with thin twice-cut fronds and round spore patches under a hood; fronds die back in winter.

species.name: Cytisus scoparius
species.tip: Green, angular-stemmed shrub with bright yellow pea flowers and small trifoliate leaves; lacks spines unlike gorse.

species.name: Dactylis glomerata
species.tip: Coarse tufted grass with dense one-sided clusters of spikelets at the ends of branches; flattened folded shoots and long ligule.

species.name: Dactylorhiza fuchsii
species.tip: Commonest British orchid of grassland and verges; pale pink to white flowers with looped, dashed lines on a three-lobed lip and spotted leaves; spike is cone-shaped.

species.name: Dactylorhiza incarnata
species.tip: Orchid of damp fens and meadows with narrow, upright, unspotted leaves hooded at the tip and flowers whose lip edges fold back; flowers vary in colour from flesh to purple.

species.name: Dactylorhiza maculata
species.tip: Small, slender spotted-orchid of acid heath and bog with pale pink flowers, a rounded shallow-lobed lip with the middle lobe tiny, and short spotted leaves.

species.name: Dactylorhiza praetermissa
species.tip: Stout marsh-orchid of damp lowland meadows, dunes and fens with unspotted or lightly spotted broad leaves and a dense head of deep magenta flowers with a broad lip.

species.name: Dactylorhiza purpurella
species.tip: Marsh-orchid of northern wet meadows, deep purple flowers with a diamond-shaped lip and dark flower stalks and bracts; leaves are unspotted or ringed with spots, shorter than Southern.

species.name: Danthonia decumbens
species.tip: Short grass of heaths with few large spikelets in a sparse panicle, no awns, and a ligule of hairs; leaves have long hairs at the base.

species.name: Daphne laureola
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with glossy, leathery oval leaves in tufts at the shoot tips, small green flowers, and black berries; shaded woods on calcareous soils, winter flowering.

species.name: Datura stramonium
species.tip: Rank, foul-smelling annual of waste ground with large trumpet-shaped white or purplish flowers and spiny, egg-shaped seed capsules; poisonous, with coarsely toothed leaves.

species.name: Daucus carota
species.tip: Umbels with divided, three-pronged bracts below and often a single dark red central floret; bird's-nest shape in fruit; found on chalk and coastal grassland.

species.name: Deschampsia cespitosa
species.tip: Big tussocks with very sharp-ridged leaves rough to the touch, and a large airy silvery-purple panicle of small spikelets with a short awn.

species.name: Digitalis purpurea
species.tip: Tall spike of nodding, tubular purple-pink flowers spotted inside, above a rosette of large downy leaves. Woodland clearings, heaths and banks; the only large tubular purple spire in this family.

species.name: Diplotaxis muralis
species.tip: Yellow flowers with dark veins on walls and railway tracks; leaves lobed and mainly in a basal rosette, with a leafless-looking stem and strong smell.

species.name: Dipsacus fullonum
species.tip: Very tall prickly biennial with egg-shaped spiny heads and long curved bracts, flowering as a purple ring; basal leaves form water-holding cups; rough grassland and verges.

species.name: Doronicum pardalianches
species.tip: Early-flowering plant with large yellow daisies and big heart-shaped basal leaves, clasping stem leaves. Naturalised in woods and shady verges, spring and early summer.

species.name: Drosera rotundifolia
species.tip: Insect-eating plant of bogs with a rosette of round red sticky-haired leaves; small white flowers on a slender spike, summer, in acid wet moors.

species.name: Dryopteris affinis
species.tip: Golden-brown scaly stalk and glossy leathery fronds with blunt, toothed tips of pinnules near the tip; darker spot at pinnule bases; woods and hedgebanks.

species.name: Dryopteris carthusiana
species.tip: Pale green, triangular, finely divided fronds held at an angle, with pale scales on stalk; damp woods and fens, rarer than Broad Buckler-fern.

species.name: Dryopteris dilatata
species.tip: Large spreading arching fronds with darker central blotch on scales and dark-centred stalk scales; widespread in woods, the commonest buckler-fern.

species.name: Dryopteris filix-mas
species.tip: Shuttlecock of tall dull green fronds with rounded pinnule tips and a dark spot where pinnules join the midrib; common in woods and hedgerows.

species.name: Echinochloa crus-galli
species.tip: Warm-season annual weed with a head made of several short, dense, one-sided racemes, often purplish; no ligule at all, which helps identify it.

species.name: Echium vulgare
species.tip: Bristly plant with spikes of funnel-shaped flowers, pink in bud turning bright blue, with protruding red stamens. Dry grassland, dunes and chalk.

species.name: Eleocharis multicaulis
species.tip: Slender spike-rush of wet heaths and bogs, one brown spikelet per stem; stems many, thin and round; the sheath mouth is oblique and reddish.

species.name: Eleocharis palustris
species.tip: Leafless round green stems, each with a single large oval brown spikelet; creeping in shallow water and wet ground; the stem is smooth and ridged when dry.

species.name: Eleocharis quinqueflora
species.tip: Short stiff stems with a single small dark brown spikelet of few flowers on damp base-rich ground; lowest scale clasps the spikelet's base completely.

species.name: Eleogiton fluitans
species.tip: Aquatic plant with thin, soft floating leaves in pools and ditches; tiny single spikelet at stem tips; stems trail and root; looks like a slender mat of green threads.

species.name: Elodea canadensis
species.tip: Submerged plant with whorls of three blunt, rather broad dark leaves that curve back; leaves widest near the middle and less pointed than in Nuttalls Waterweed.

species.name: Elodea nuttallii
species.tip: Submerged plant with whorls of three narrow, pointed, strongly curved leaves, paler and softer than Canadian Waterweed; common in ponds and canals, spreading in recent decades.

species.name: Elymus athericus
species.tip: Stiff, bluish-green couch of salt marsh edges with a flat spike of spikelets set edge-on in two rows; leaves rolled and ribbed on top.

species.name: Elymus caninus
species.tip: Tufted couch of woods and hedges with an arching spike and long awns on the spikelets; no creeping rhizomes unlike Common Couch.

species.name: Elymus junceiformis
species.tip: Blue-grey stiff couch of foredunes with a brittle spike, spikelets overlapping and unawned; leaves rolled and ribbed above, creeping by rhizomes.

species.name: Elymus repens
species.tip: Creeping weed forming patches with a flat two-rowed spike; narrow claw-like auricles at the leaf base and white rhizomes distinguish it.

species.name: Empetrum nigrum
species.tip: Low evergreen with needle-like leaves grooved beneath, tiny pinkish flowers in leaf axils and black berries; moorland and mountain heath, unlike heathers.

species.name: Epilobium brunnescens
species.tip: Tiny mat-forming willowherb with creeping rooting stems, rounded little leaves and solitary small flowers; common on paths, walls and rocky ground, mostly in the north and west.

species.name: Epilobium ciliatum
species.tip: Upright, often branching willowherb with narrow leaves, small pale pink flowers and glandular hairs on the upper stem; the seed pods are glandular too. Common weed of gardens and waste ground.

species.name: Epilobium hirsutum
species.tip: Tall, stout, softly hairy willowherb of ditches and streamsides with large rose-pink flowers and a four-lobed stigma; leaves clasp the stem and smell faintly fruity.

species.name: Epilobium montanum
species.tip: Common willowherb of shady places and walls with short-stalked or unstalked, broad, opposite oval leaves, small pink flowers with a four-lobed stigma and a rounded, hairy stem.

species.name: Epilobium obscurum
species.tip: Slender willowherb of damp ground with a stem bearing raised lines, small pink flowers and short pods; leaves are narrow, stalkless and often reddish. Spreads by leafy runners in autumn.
